title: A Change Is a Price and a Date, Agreed Before the Work Is Done
summary: Every change on a construction job carries two prices: money and time. This lesson defines change orders, change directives and claims, explains notice and time bars, sorts delay into excusable, compensable, non-excusable and concurrent, and introduces the time impact analysis and the recovery schedule.
body:
A change is not finished when the price is agreed; it is finished when the price and the date are both agreed, in writing, before the work proceeds. Everything else becomes a claim.

Recall

Q. In a pay application with a retainage step-down, what happens to retainage once measured work passes the halfway mark?

A. Further retainage stops on new work, but what was already held stays held. After the step-down, nearly every dollar of new measured work is paid in full, so measurement matters more, not less.

Q. What should a nonconformance report record?

A. What does not meet the specification, the proposed disposition, such as repair, replace or accept with engineering approval, who approved it, and the evidence that the disposition was carried out.

Q. What is the difference between bearing capacity and settlement in a shallow foundation?

A. Bearing capacity is the pressure at which the ground would fail in shear. Settlement is how far the foundation moves downward under service load. A footing can be safe in bearing and still settle too much, so both must be checked.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Petra joins me this week because changes and delay are the same problem seen from two sides: the cost side and the schedule side. On almost every project something will change: the design develops, the ground surprises you, a buyer wants an upgrade, a supplier slips. Each change is an ordinary event. What decides whether it stays ordinary is how fast and how completely you price it, in money and in days. Owners who manage changes well finish close to budget and on a defensible date. Owners who do not face a claim at the end that rewrites both.

Three words that mean different things

In plain English, there are three ways extra work arrives. Both sides agree what it costs and how long it takes. Or you need it done now and you will agree the price later. Or the contractor says it is owed something and you disagree.

The professional names follow. A change order is a written agreement signed by owner and contractor that changes the scope, the contract sum, the contract time, or all three. A construction change directive, a term used in the American Institute of Architects forms, is the owner's written instruction to proceed with changed work before price or time is agreed, with a method for fixing them later. A claim is a demand by one party for money, time or both that the other has not accepted. Week 49 taught change control as a scope discipline. This week it becomes a time discipline as well.

Worked example, hypothetical round numbers. You change the facade panel specification in month 7. The contractor prices the direct cost at 300,000 dollars and says it adds 15 days to the critical path, the longest chain of linked activities that sets the completion date. Extended general conditions, the contractor's time-related site costs such as supervision, site offices and equipment, run at 8,000 dollars a day. Fifteen days is 120,000 dollars. The true price of your change is 420,000 dollars and 15 days, and the change order must say both. A change order that prices the panels at 300,000 dollars and is silent on time leaves the 15 days and the 120,000 dollars to be argued at the end, usually with interest and a lawyer.

Notice and time bars

Most construction contracts require a party who believes it is entitled to more time or money to give written notice within a stated period after it becomes aware of the event. Many go further and say that a claim not notified in time is barred. That is a time bar. The purpose is fairness to the other side: the owner needs to know early, while it can still change the design, accelerate, or decide the work is not worth doing.

Notice runs both ways. You, as owner, may have to give notice of defective work, of a claim for liquidated damages, the pre-agreed daily amount the contractor pays for late completion, or of your own disputes with the contractor's claims. Week 77 introduced conditions precedent and time bars in the standard forms. The practical rule is that every notice you receive is logged on the day it arrives and answered in writing within the contract period, and every event that might entitle you to something gets a notice from you, even when the relationship is good.

Say that out loud now.

Every notice is logged the day it arrives and answered in writing inside the contract period, without exception.

Four kinds of delay

Delay is classified by who bears the risk of its cause. Excusable but non-compensable delay, such as weather worse than the contract assumed, or a genuine force majeure event, gives the contractor more time but no money. Excusable and compensable delay, caused by the owner or its design team, such as late approvals, late information or owner changes, gives time and money. Non-excusable delay, the contractor's own slow work, gives neither, and the contractor pays liquidated damages if completion is late. Concurrent delay is when an owner-caused and a contractor-caused delay affect the critical path at the same time; how it is treated depends on the contract and the law, which LEX covers on Day 4.

Only delay to the critical path moves the completion date. Delay to an activity with float, the spare time an activity has before it delays completion, may cost money but not time. That is why every delay argument is in the end a schedule argument.

Second worked example. In one month the site loses 8 days to rain beyond the contract's normal allowance, the owner's engineer returns a key shop drawing 12 days late, and the contractor's steel arrives 6 days late. If the rain and the late drawing both hit critical activities in separate weeks, and the steel delay ran in parallel with the late drawing, a defensible analysis might give 8 days of time only for weather, 12 days of time and money for the drawing, and treat the steel as concurrent with the drawing for those 6 days. The exact answer depends on the contract and the evidence. The point is that you cannot answer it at all without an updated schedule.

Measuring delay and recovering from it

A time impact analysis models the effect of a delay event by inserting a short network of new activities, called a fragnet, into the most recent updated schedule and recalculating the completion date. Done at the time of the event, it is a forward-looking estimate that both parties can agree. Done years later by experts, it becomes a battle.

A recovery schedule is the contractor's plan to win back lost time, by resequencing, adding crews or working longer hours. If the delay is the contractor's, recovery is its cost. If the owner instructs the contractor to keep the original date despite an excusable delay, that is directed acceleration and the owner pays. If the owner refuses a justified extension and insists on the date without saying so, many legal systems allow a claim for constructive acceleration [unverified — confirm independently].

How the best do it

Disciplined owners and contractors run a live change log reviewed weekly, price every change for cost and time within days rather than months, require a time impact analysis with every change request that claims time, and update the schedule monthly against actual progress. A small developer can copy this with one spreadsheet, a monthly schedule update from the contractor and a rule that no change order is signed without a time line.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: whether change costs and claim settlements are added to the cost of the building or treated otherwise depends on local rules; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: an unanswered notice can become an admission or a waiver. Banking: the lender's monitor reviews changes against contingency, and an unpriced delay shortens the interest reserve. Governance: set written authority limits for who may sign a change order and up to what value. Estate: a live claim is a contingent liability or asset that must be recorded. Exit: a buyer or refinancing lender will ask about open claims, and unresolved ones discount the price.

Professional sign-off required: construction lawyer, on notice and claims provisions; scheduling consultant, on time impact analysis; quantity surveyor, on the pricing of changes.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is pricing changes for money and leaving time for later. Time is where the expensive part lives. The control is a rule that no change order is signed without a stated effect on the contract time, supported by a time impact analysis on the current schedule.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks a good relationship makes notices unnecessary. Good relationships end at the final account, and the notice log is what both sides will rely on then.

Callback

In Week 50, Petra taught that float is a shared resource, that who owns it should be written into the contract, and that a baseline schedule must be reviewed before it is accepted. This week puts that to work. When an owner change consumes float, whether it delays completion depends on who owns the float, and you only know that if you decided it before the first change arrived.

Recap

A change carries a price and a date. Change orders agree both, change directives order work first, and claims are disputes. Notice must be given and answered on time. Delay is excusable, compensable, non-excusable or concurrent, and only critical path delay moves completion. Measure it with a time impact analysis on a live schedule.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: a composite case of notices nobody answered.
checklist: No change order is signed without a stated effect on cost and on contract time.
Every change request that claims time comes with a time impact analysis on the current schedule.
Every notice received is logged on the day it arrives.
Every notice is answered in writing inside the contract period.
I give my own notices on time, even when the relationship is good.
The contractor updates the schedule monthly against actual progress.
Written authority limits say who may sign a change and up to what value.
I classify every delay event as excusable, compensable, non-excusable or concurrent as it happens.
head: Field checklist
speak: A change carries two prices: money and time. A change order agrees both in writing. A change directive tells the contractor to proceed before the price is fixed. A claim is a demand the other side has not accepted. Most contracts require written notice of a claim within a set period, and many bar late claims, so I log every notice the day it arrives and answer it in writing inside the contract period. Delay comes in four kinds: excusable but not compensable, like abnormal weather, which gives time only; excusable and compensable, caused by me or my designers, which gives time and money; non-excusable, the contractor's own, which gives neither; and concurrent, when both happen at once. Only delay to the critical path moves completion. So every change that claims time comes with a time impact analysis on the current schedule, and no change order is signed without a date line.
terms: Change order — a written agreement signed by owner and contractor changing scope, contract sum, contract time or all three.
Time bar — a contract term under which a claim not notified within a stated period is lost.
Time impact analysis — a method of measuring a delay's effect by inserting a fragnet of new activities into the current schedule and recalculating completion.

hostile.q: You signed eleven change orders on this job and not one says anything about time. Why should I believe the completion date in your draw report?
hostile.a: You should not, yet, and I will fix it. I have asked the contractor for a time impact analysis on each of the eleven against the current update, and I am recording our position on each in writing this week. From today no change order is signed without a time line. You will have a reconciled completion date and its cost effect on the interest reserve within two weeks.

title: The Notices Nobody Answered
summary: A composite case: a contractor sent written delay notices that the owner's team never logged or answered, while the owner insisted on the original date. The contractor accelerated, then claimed for constructive acceleration and extended costs. With no contemporaneous analysis, the owner lost its concurrency defence and paid. Seven forensic steps and one rule follow.
rule: Rule 118: Answer every notice in writing inside the contract period, keep an updated schedule that can measure delay as it happens, and price time with every change before the work proceeds.
body:
This is a composite example. The owner did not lose this claim because the contractor was right about everything; it lost because it had no record of its own, and silence had answered the notices for it.

Recall

Q. What is the difference between directed and constructive acceleration?

A. Directed acceleration is an owner instructing the contractor to finish earlier than it is entitled to. Constructive acceleration arises when the owner refuses a justified extension and insists on the original date, so the contractor speeds up to avoid liquidated damages.

Q. Why collect unconditional waivers for last month's payment rather than this month's?

A. Because an unconditional waiver releases lien rights on signing. It should only cover money already received; for money about to be paid, a conditional waiver is correct.

Q. What is a hold point that work passed without release?

A. A nonconformance, whatever the quality of the work, because the inspection that should have happened before the work was covered did not.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Cole joins me because this is a case about records as much as construction. It is a composite, built from patterns that recur in delay disputes. The numbers are hypothetical round figures. I chose it because the failure is entirely within an owner's control and costs nothing to prevent.

1. Timeline

A developer builds a 40,000,000 dollar mid-rise residential project on an 18-month contract with liquidated damages of 10,000 dollars a day. In month 4 the design team issues revised structural drawings for the transfer level, the floor where column loads are redirected. In month 5 the contractor sends a written notice by email to the owner's project manager saying the revisions will delay the frame. It sends further notices in months 6 and 8, each with a short narrative. Nobody logs them. Nobody replies. In month 9 the owner's monthly meeting minutes record that the owner "expects the contract completion date to be met." The contractor adds a second shift on the frame and weekend work on the envelope. The building finishes 40 days late. The owner deducts 400,000 dollars of liquidated damages. The contractor claims 1,600,000 dollars for acceleration costs and extended general conditions, and an extension of 60 days. The dispute goes to arbitration.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions mattered. Issuing the structural revisions without a time impact analysis of their own. Leaving the contractor's notices unanswered, so the contractor's account of events stood alone. And recording an expectation that the original date be met while a justified extension was pending, which is exactly the fact pattern of constructive acceleration.

3. Assumptions

The owner's team assumed the notices were posturing, because the contractor had also been slow on its own curtain wall. It assumed that it could argue concurrency later. It assumed that liquidated damages were automatic once completion was late. And it assumed that email notices to one person did not count because the contract mentioned delivery to a named address. The tribunal treated the owner's conduct and its later reliance on the same email channel as relevant to that point; how strictly notice provisions are applied varies by contract and law.

4. Incentives

The owner's project manager was rewarded for holding the date and the budget, so acknowledging a delay felt like failure. The design team did not want its late revisions examined. The contractor had an incentive to build a careful paper record, because it knew a claim was coming. Only one side was paying attention to the evidence.

Say that out loud now.

An unanswered notice is not ignored. It is answered by silence, and silence is evidence.

5. Warning signs ignored

Three written notices in four months. Late drawing revisions on the transfer level, which sits on the critical path of almost any frame. A second shift appearing on site without an instruction from the owner. Monthly schedule updates showing the frame finishing later each month while the completion date on the summary page never moved. Each of these said that a claim was being built.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was the month 9 meeting. Up to then, the owner could have answered the notices, commissioned its own time impact analysis, granted a reasoned partial extension, or formally instructed acceleration on agreed terms. Once it recorded an expectation that the original date be met, with three unanswered notices on file, it had handed the contractor the strongest version of its case.

7. Root cause

The root cause was the absence of a notice and change control system. The owner had no log, no response discipline, no contemporaneous schedule analysis and no rule that changes be priced for time. Every later problem flowed from that.

What the owner's reply should have looked like

The fix was never a long letter. A reply to the month 5 notice, sent within the contract period, could have been five sentences: "We acknowledge your notice dated the 12th regarding the transfer-level revisions. We do not yet accept that they affect the completion date. Please provide, within 14 days, a time impact analysis on the current update showing the claimed effect on the critical path. We reserve all our rights, including under the notice provisions. We will respond in full within 14 days of receiving it." That reply does four jobs. It proves receipt, it keeps the owner's position open, it demands the analysis that will decide the question, and it starts a clock of the owner's own. Three such replies would have changed the whole case.

Cole's view: why the concurrency defence failed

Mr Shabazz, the owner had a real argument. The contractor's curtain wall was late too, and if that delay ran in parallel with the frame delay, the owner might have avoided paying for some of the extended costs. But concurrency must be proved, usually with a window-by-window analysis on schedule updates made at the time. The owner had never analysed the updates. Its expert reconstructed them years later, and the contractor's expert pointed out every assumption. A tribunal will generally prefer the analysis built on contemporaneous records.

The worked example of the cost. The settlement, reached after the hearing on liability, gave the contractor most of its extension and a large share of its extended costs, and the owner refunded most of the liquidated damages. On these hypothetical numbers, suppose the owner ended up paying 1,100,000 dollars plus refunding 300,000 dollars, against a position that a timely analysis might have settled at a fraction of that, plus its own legal and expert fees. A second worked example shows what prevention costs: a monthly schedule review by a scheduling consultant, perhaps 3,000 to 5,000 dollars a month on a job this size as a practitioner estimate, totals well under 100,000 dollars over 18 months.

Professional sign-off required: construction lawyer, on notice and claims procedure; scheduling consultant, on delay analysis.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating notices as relationship noise rather than legal events. The control is a notice log, a named person responsible for it, and a written response to every notice inside the contract period, even if the response is only that the owner reserves its position and requests particulars.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner believes liquidated damages are self-executing. Liquidated damages depend on the completion date being right, and the completion date depends on extensions being decided properly.

Callback

In Week 82, Vera taught that contemporaneous records beat recollection, and that the time to create a record is when the event happens. This case is that lesson with a price on it. The contractor's notices were contemporaneous; the owner's defence was reconstructed.

Recap

In this composite, an owner left three delay notices unanswered, issued drawing revisions without a time analysis, and insisted on the original date. It lost its liquidated damages and paid acceleration and extended costs. Rule 118: answer every notice in writing, keep a live schedule that measures delay as it happens, and price time with every change.

Next: Roman on The Money: what delay really costs, day by day, and how the lender's clock runs.
checklist: I keep a notice log with a named owner.
Every notice gets a written response inside the contract period.
My response to a notice I dispute reserves my position and requests particulars.
My own design revisions get a time impact analysis before issue.
A scheduling consultant reviews each monthly update for slippage.
I never record an expectation of the original date while an extension is pending without legal advice.
I note unexplained extra shifts or weekend work as a sign a claim is being built.
I prepare any concurrency argument month by month, not at the end.
head: Field checklist
speak: This is a composite case. An owner issued revised structural drawings in month 4 without analysing their effect on time. The contractor sent written delay notices in months 5, 6 and 8. Nobody logged or answered them. In month 9 the minutes recorded that the owner expected the original date to be met. The contractor added a second shift, finished 40 days late, and claimed acceleration costs and extended general conditions. The owner had a real concurrency argument, because the contractor's curtain wall was also late, but it had never analysed the monthly updates, so its defence was reconstructed years later and lost to the contractor's contemporaneous record. The root cause was no notice and change control system at all. Rule 118: answer every notice in writing inside the contract period, keep an updated schedule that can measure delay as it happens, and price time with every change before the work proceeds.
terms: Concurrent delay — an owner-caused and a contractor-caused delay affecting the critical path in the same period, treated differently by different contracts and laws.
Window analysis — a delay analysis that divides the project into periods and measures the critical path delay in each, usually from contemporaneous schedule updates.
Reservation of rights — a written statement that a party does not accept a position and keeps its rights open, while the matter is examined.

hostile.q: Your contractor has three delay notices on file and you never answered one. Why should I fund your counterclaim for liquidated damages?
hostile.a: You should judge it on the analysis, not on my past silence, which I accept was a failure. I have commissioned an independent window analysis on the monthly updates, and I will separate the owner-caused delay we owe for from the contractor's own curtain wall delay. Where we owe time and money we will say so and settle it. The counterclaim covers only what the analysis supports.

title: What Delay Really Costs: The Daily Burn and the Lender's Clock
summary: Delay has a daily price made of interest, extended site costs, owner costs and lost income, and liquidated damages rarely cover all of it. This lesson builds a daily delay cost, compares it with liquidated damages and acceleration, and shows what a slipping date does to the interest reserve, the loan maturity and the return.
body:
Every day of delay late in a project costs more than any day before it, because the loan is nearly fully drawn and the income has not started; know that number before you argue about who pays it.

Recall

Q. What is a fragnet?

A. A short network of new activities representing a delay event or change, inserted into the current schedule to calculate its effect on completion in a time impact analysis.

Q. What does a gap in last month's unconditional waivers warn you about?

A. That money you paid the contractor may not have reached the trades, which is an early sign of a cash flow problem and a lien risk.

Q. What is ground improvement, in one sentence?

A. Treating weak soil in place, for example by compaction, preloading or stone columns, so that it can carry a shallow foundation within acceptable settlement instead of switching to deep foundations.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the lender looks at delay as a credit event. When a completion date slips, the interest reserve drains faster than planned, the loan may approach its maturity before the building is stabilised, and the cost-overrun and carry guarantees come closer to being called. You need to know your daily delay cost cold, because every decision this week, whether to accelerate, whether to settle, whether to grant an extension, is a comparison against it.

Building the daily delay cost

In plain English: add up everything that costs money for every extra day the building is not finished. The professional framing breaks it into owner-side components, because the contractor's extended general conditions are a separate claim against you.

Worked example, hypothetical round numbers. The construction loan is 30,000,000 dollars, 27,000,000 drawn near completion, at 7 percent a year. Daily interest: 27,000,000 times 0.07, divided by 365, is about 5,180 dollars. The building is expected to produce stabilised net operating income, rent less operating costs, of 2,400,000 dollars a year, but delay pushes the whole lease-up back; the income lost from the start of operations is 2,400,000 divided by 365, about 6,580 dollars a day once you are in the stabilised period, and less during lease-up, so use a weighted figure of perhaps 3,000 dollars a day for the first months. Owner's staff, consultants, insurance extensions and security: 1,200 dollars a day. Total owner daily delay cost: roughly 5,180 plus 3,000 plus 1,200, which is about 9,380 dollars a day. Sixty days of delay is about 563,000 dollars before any contractor claim.

Liquidated damages rarely make you whole

Liquidated damages are a pre-agreed daily sum the contractor pays for late completion. In many legal systems they must be a genuine pre-estimate of loss or a legitimate protection of the owner's interest, not a penalty, to be enforceable [unverified — confirm independently]. They are also usually the owner's only remedy for delay, and contractors negotiate them down or cap them, often at a percentage of the contract sum as a commercial practice, not a standard.

In the example, suppose liquidated damages are 5,000 dollars a day, capped. Your real cost is about 9,380. On a contractor-caused delay of 60 days, you recover 300,000 dollars and lose 563,000 dollars: a gap of about 263,000 dollars you carry. On an owner-caused delay, you recover nothing and also pay the contractor's extended general conditions, say 8,000 dollars a day, so 60 days costs you about 563,000 plus 480,000, over 1,000,000 dollars. That asymmetry is why preventing owner-caused delay is worth more than pursuing contractor-caused delay.

Say that out loud now.

My daily delay cost is a number I know, and owner-caused delay costs me about twice what contractor delay does.

Accelerate, absorb or argue

When the date slips, there are three choices. Accelerate: pay for more crews or hours to win back time. Absorb: accept the delay and its cost. Argue: dispute who caused it. The money test is simple. Second worked example: the contractor offers to recover 30 days for 300,000 dollars of acceleration cost on an owner-caused delay. Thirty days of your delay cost is about 281,000 dollars plus 240,000 dollars of extended general conditions you would otherwise owe, about 521,000 in all. Paying 300,000 to avoid 521,000 is worth it, if the recovery is real. The control is to pay acceleration against milestones achieved, not in advance, and to record it as a change order with a revised date so there is no later argument about whether the acceleration was directed.

The lender's clock

Three clocks run on the loan. The interest reserve: sized for a planned schedule, it runs out early if completion slips, and then interest must come from equity. The in-balance test: a delay that increases cost to complete can push the loan out of balance and stop draws. And maturity: a construction loan usually matures on a date that assumes completion and lease-up; if delay pushes stabilisation past maturity, you need an extension, which usually costs a fee and may come with tighter terms. Each of these is commercial practice that varies by lender.

Third worked example: an interest reserve sized at 2,000,000 dollars for a 20-month build with a 4-month cushion. A 3-month delay late in the job at about 5,180 dollars a day consumes roughly 466,000 dollars of reserve that was meant for lease-up. Tell the lender before the reserve is short, with the recalculated reserve and the source of any top-up.

What delay does to the return

Delay hurts the internal rate of return in two ways at once: costs rise and the positive cash flows arrive later. On a typical development, a few months of delay can take several points off the levered return, because the equity is fully invested throughout. Run your model with the completion date as a variable and know the cost of each month.

Put the daily delay cost on the first page of your monthly report, beside the forecast completion date. When the date moves by a week, the report should say what that week cost, in dollars, without anyone asking. That habit does two things. It makes delay visible to your partners and lender as a number rather than a feeling, and it trains your own team to treat every lost day as money, which is what it is. A small developer can do this with one cell in a spreadsheet, refreshed when the drawn balance or the lease-up forecast changes.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

On a personal balance sheet, delay is a liquidity event and a guarantee event. If you have signed a carry guarantee, you may be personally liable for interest and operating shortfalls until stabilisation, so each month of delay is a month of contingent personal liability. Keep a personal liquidity reserve that would cover the carry you have guaranteed for a realistic delay, and treat any guarantee as a liability on your own balance sheet, not a footnote. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal financial decision.

Professional sign-off required: lender's counsel and your own lawyer, on liquidated damages, extension and maturity terms; quantity surveyor, on acceleration pricing.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is arguing about who caused a delay before knowing what it costs. The control is a daily delay cost calculated at financial close and refreshed quarterly, used to decide every acceleration and settlement.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner sets liquidated damages by copying another contract, then discovers they cover half his real loss. Set them from your own daily cost, with legal advice on enforceability.

Callback

In Week 44, I taught stress tests and break-evens: the question of how far a variable can move before the deal breaks. Completion date is one of the most powerful variables in a development model. This lesson gives it a daily price, which is the input to that stress test.

Recap

Delay costs interest, lost income and owner costs every day, rising as the loan fills. Liquidated damages rarely cover it, and owner-caused delay costs about twice as much because you also pay the contractor's extended costs. Compare acceleration with the delay cost, pay for it on milestones, and tell the lender before the reserve runs short.

Next: LEX on The Rules: how contracts and courts read notice, time bars and concurrent delay.
checklist: I calculate my owner daily delay cost at financial close.
I refresh the daily delay cost each quarter as the loan draws down.
I set liquidated damages from my own cost, with legal advice on enforceability.
I compare every acceleration offer against the delay cost it avoids.
I pay acceleration on milestones achieved, recorded as a change order with a revised date.
I recalculate the interest reserve whenever the completion date moves.
I check the loan maturity against the latest stabilisation date.
I hold a personal liquidity reserve against any carry guarantee I have signed.
head: Field checklist
speak: Every day of delay late in a project costs more than any day before it, because the loan is nearly fully drawn and income has not started. In this hypothetical, interest on 27,000,000 dollars at 7 percent is about 5,180 dollars a day. Add lost income during lease-up and owner costs, and the owner's delay cost is about 9,380 dollars a day. Liquidated damages of 5,000 a day leave a gap on contractor delay. On owner-caused delay I recover nothing and also pay the contractor's extended general conditions, so it costs me roughly twice as much. That is why preventing owner delay is worth more than pursuing contractor delay. When the date slips, I compare acceleration with the delay it avoids, and pay for it against milestones. And I watch three lender clocks: the interest reserve, the in-balance test and the loan maturity, telling the lender early.
terms: Liquidated damages — a pre-agreed daily sum the contractor pays the owner for late completion, usually the owner's only remedy for delay.
Extended general conditions — the contractor's time-related site costs, such as supervision and site facilities, for each extra day on site.
Carry guarantee — a guarantor's promise to pay interest and operating shortfalls until the project is stabilised.

hostile.q: Completion has slipped three months. Your interest reserve was sized for the original date. When does it run out, and who pays after that?
hostile.a: On the current forecast it runs out about seven weeks before the revised completion. I have recalculated it at the actual drawn balance and rate, and the shortfall of about 466,000 dollars will be deposited from equity before it is needed, not after. I am also sending the acceleration proposal we have priced, which, if it works, recovers 30 days for less than those days would cost us.

title: Notice, Time Bars and Concurrent Delay: How Contracts and Courts Read Them
summary: Notice provisions, time bars, no-damages-for-delay clauses and the treatment of concurrent delay are where construction claims are actually decided. This lesson explains each as a concept, notes how different standard forms and legal traditions approach them, and shows why the written record decides most of them.
body:
Most delay disputes are not decided by who was slower; they are decided by what the contract says about notice and concurrency, and by whose records prove what happened.

Recall

Q. In the delay cost lesson, why does owner-caused delay cost the owner about twice as much as contractor-caused delay?

A. Because on owner-caused delay the owner bears its own daily cost and also pays the contractor's extended general conditions, while on contractor-caused delay it at least recovers liquidated damages.

Q. What is a lien waiver form problem in a statutory state?

A. Some states prescribe the waiver wording and treat a non-conforming form as ineffective, so a waiver copied from elsewhere may not protect title.

Q. What does a geotechnical report's recommended allowable bearing pressure already include?

A. A factor of safety against bearing failure and, usually, a limit chosen to keep settlement acceptable, which is why it is a design value and not the ground's ultimate strength.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a claim can be right on the facts and lost on the contract, or weak on the facts and won because the other side did not follow procedure. Owners lose claims they should win and pay claims they should not because they treat these clauses as boilerplate. I will teach the concepts. Applying them to your contract, in your jurisdiction, is a job for a construction lawyer licensed there.

Notice provisions and conditions precedent

A notice provision says what a party must do, in writing, by when, to whom and with what detail, to claim time or money. When the contract makes notice a condition precedent, the right to the claim depends on the notice being given as specified. The standard forms take different approaches. The American Institute of Architects form used for general conditions, A201, sets a short claims notice period measured in days from the event or from when the claimant recognised it. The FIDIC forms used internationally require notice within a fixed number of days, commonly cited as 28 in their standard text, and say that a claim not notified in time loses its entitlement. ConsensusDocs takes its own approach. Read the exact edition in your contract; verify against the current adopted edition before relying on any period.

A worked example in concept. A contractor discovers on day 1 that a late owner approval will delay the frame. It gives written notice on day 35 under a contract that requires notice within 21 days as a condition precedent. On a strict reading the claim is barred. Whether a court or tribunal applies it strictly depends on the governing law and the facts, including whether the owner already knew, whether it was prejudiced, and how it behaved.

Waiver by conduct and the duty to respond

An owner who repeatedly considers late claims on their merits, negotiates them, or pays some of them, may be found to have waived strict compliance with the time bar [unverified — confirm independently]. So if you intend to rely on a time bar, say so in writing promptly, while still reserving your position on the merits. The same logic applies to informal routes: if the contract requires notice to a named person at a named address, and your team habitually deals with notices sent by email to the project manager, a tribunal may give weight to that habit. Equally, a contract may require the owner to respond to a claim within a period; failure to respond can, under some forms, have consequences of its own. The habit to build is a written response to every notice, inside the period, stating your position.

Say that out loud now.

If I mean to rely on a time bar, I say so in writing at once, and I never negotiate a late claim without reserving my rights.

The prevention principle and no-damages-for-delay clauses

Many common law systems recognise some form of the prevention principle: a party cannot insist on a deadline that its own conduct prevented the other from meeting. If the owner causes delay and the contract has no mechanism to extend time for it, the owner may lose the right to liquidated damages altogether, leaving it to prove its general damages instead [unverified — confirm independently]. That is one reason well-drafted contracts include an extension of time mechanism for owner-caused delay: it protects the owner's liquidated damages as much as the contractor.

A no-damages-for-delay clause says the contractor's only remedy for delay, even owner-caused, is more time, not money. Enforceability varies widely: many courts in the United States enforce them but recognise exceptions, such as delay not contemplated by the parties, active interference or bad faith, and some states limit them by statute, particularly on public work [unverified — confirm independently]. Do not rely on one without local advice.

Concurrent delay

When owner and contractor delays overlap on the critical path, there are broadly three approaches. One gives the contractor time but no money for the concurrent period: it escapes liquidated damages, but does not recover its own costs. Another apportions the delay and its costs between the parties according to causation. A third tests which delay was truly dominant. Different legal traditions and contracts lean toward different approaches, and some contracts state the rule expressly. The Society of Construction Law Delay and Disruption Protocol, published in the United Kingdom, is widely used as guidance and favours time without money for true concurrency in many cases, but it is guidance, not law. AACE International publishes recommended practices on forensic schedule analysis that are widely cited for method. Verify against the current editions.

A second worked example in concept. The owner's late transfer-level drawings and the contractor's late curtain wall both delay completion in months 6 to 8. If your contract says concurrent delay gives time but not money, the contractor gets an extension for that window and you lose liquidated damages for it, but you do not pay its extended costs. If the contract is silent, the answer depends on governing law, and the expert analyses will decide what was truly concurrent. That is why it is worth writing the rule into the contract at award.

Differing site conditions

Many contracts include a clause allocating the risk of subsurface or concealed conditions materially different from those indicated or ordinarily expected. Under such clauses, a contractor that encounters them and gives prompt notice may be entitled to time and money, which encourages lower bids because contractors need not price the unknown. Without such a clause, the risk often stays with the contractor, and bids rise. Week 78 covered unforeseen ground as a risk allocation choice; here the point is that the notice requirement applies to it with full force.

Professional sign-off required: construction lawyer licensed in the governing jurisdiction, on notice, time bar, concurrency and delay damages clauses; scheduling consultant, on the method of delay analysis the contract specifies.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is assuming a time bar will save you while your own conduct undermines it. The control is consistency: respond to every notice in writing, invoke time bars promptly where you mean to, and never negotiate a late claim without a reservation of rights.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner deletes the extension of time clause for owner-caused delay to look tough. In many systems that can cost him his liquidated damages on the first owner-caused delay.

Callback

In Week 20, I taught that a condition precedent is an event that must happen before an obligation arises, and that whether a clause is a condition or a promise changes the remedy. Notice clauses are the most important conditions precedent you will meet on a building site. The Week 20 question, condition or promise, decides whether a late claim survives.

Recap

Notice provisions can be conditions precedent, and time bars can extinguish claims, but conduct can waive them. The prevention principle protects contractors against owner-caused deadlines, so keep an extension mechanism. No-damages-for-delay clauses and concurrency rules vary by contract and law. Write the rules into the contract, and keep the records that prove them.

Next: Petra on The Numbers: reverse engineering an extension of time from the award back to the schedule.
checklist: I know the notice period, form and recipient in my contract and edition.
I know whether notice is a condition precedent.
I invoke a time bar in writing promptly when I mean to rely on it.
I never negotiate a late claim without a written reservation of rights.
My contract includes an extension mechanism for owner-caused delay.
I take local advice before relying on a no-damages-for-delay clause.
My contract states how concurrent delay is treated.
My contract states the differing site conditions rule and its notice requirement.
head: Field checklist
speak: Most delay disputes are decided by the contract and the records, not by who was slower. Notice provisions say what must be given, by when and to whom, and many make notice a condition precedent, so a late claim can be barred. The standard forms differ, so I read my exact edition. But an owner who negotiates late claims on their merits can waive a time bar by conduct, so if I mean to rely on it I say so in writing at once, and I reserve my rights whenever I discuss a late claim. The prevention principle means that if I cause delay and the contract has no extension mechanism, I may lose my liquidated damages, so I keep one. No-damages-for-delay clauses and the treatment of concurrent delay vary by law and contract, so I write the concurrency rule into the contract at award. A construction lawyer licensed in the governing jurisdiction signs off.
terms: Condition precedent — an event that must occur, such as timely notice, before a right or obligation arises.
Prevention principle — the common law idea that a party cannot hold the other to a deadline its own conduct prevented being met.
No-damages-for-delay clause — a term limiting the contractor's remedy for delay to more time, with no money, whose enforceability varies.

hostile.q: The contractor's claim was notified late, but your team has been negotiating it for three months. Can you still rely on the time bar?
hostile.a: I do not assume so, and my counsel is reviewing exactly that, including every letter in the negotiation. Our position is reserved in writing in each of them. If the advice is that the bar is weakened, we will assess the claim on its merits with an independent window analysis, which is the position I would rather defend anyway. You will have counsel's view in writing before the next draw.

title: Reverse Engineering an Extension of Time From the Award Back to the Schedule
summary: This lesson starts from a finished outcome, an award of 25 days of extension, 15 of them compensable, with 10 days of liquidated damages, and works backward to the schedule analysis, the records and the daily rates that produced it. Every step uses hypothetical round numbers and shows which record each figure depends on.
body:
Every number in a delay settlement traces back to a schedule update, a daily record and a contract rate; work backward from the award and you learn exactly which records you must create while the job is running.

Recall

Q. What does the prevention principle protect against?

A. An owner holding a contractor to a deadline that the owner's own conduct prevented it from meeting. It is a reason to keep an extension mechanism for owner-caused delay in the contract.

Q. In the worked pay application, what was the two-way arithmetic check?

A. Contract sum less earned-less-retainage must equal remaining work plus retainage held. If the two sides differ, there is an error on the page.

Q. What is the purpose of a field density test in earthworks?

A. To confirm each compacted layer of fill reached the specified density compared with a laboratory reference, before the next layer covers it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is an even week, so we reverse engineer. We start with a finished outcome, as you might read it in a settlement agreement, and take it apart. The purpose is practical: once you see which record produced each number, you will know what to insist on from the first week of construction. All numbers are hypothetical and round. The contract rates are commercial terms for illustration, not standards.

The outcome

The settlement reads: the contractor is granted an extension of time of 25 calendar days. Of these, 15 days are compensable at 6,000 dollars a day for extended general conditions, 90,000 dollars, in addition to the agreed direct cost of the change. The remaining 10 days of excusable delay are non-compensable. Actual completion was 35 days after the original contract date, so 10 days are the contractor's responsibility, and liquidated damages of 5,000 dollars a day apply to them: 50,000 dollars.

Step 1: the total delay

Start with dates, in calendar days from notice to proceed. The baseline schedule, reviewed and accepted before work began, set contract completion at day 500. Actual substantial completion, certified by the architect, was day 535. Total delay: 535 minus 500 equals 35 days.

Record needed: the accepted baseline schedule and the substantial completion certificate. Without an accepted baseline, there is no agreed starting line, and every later step is disputed.

Step 2: split excusable from non-excusable

The award gives 25 days, so 35 minus 25 leaves 10 days of non-excusable delay. Liquidated damages: 10 days times 5,000 dollars a day equals 50,000 dollars. Check the cap: the contract caps liquidated damages at a stated amount, which 50,000 is well below.

Notice what this step already tells you: the contractor's own share of the delay is only 10 of 35 days, so the owner's starting position of deducting 35 days of liquidated damages would have been wrong by 125,000 dollars.

Record needed: the liquidated damages clause, the cap, and the owner's notice of intention to deduct, if the contract requires one.

Step 3: the weather days

Of the 25 excused days, 10 are non-compensable. They came from weather. The contract's baseline allowed 12 rain days in the relevant months, a figure taken from historical local data and written into the schedule. Daily reports record 22 days on which rain stopped critical work. Abnormal weather: 22 minus 12 equals 10 days. Because those 10 days fell on activities on the critical path at the time, they extend completion by 10 days, time only.

Records needed: the contract's weather allowance, daily site reports signed at the time showing which activities were stopped, and the schedule update showing those activities were critical. A daily report that says only "rain" is weak. One that says "rain from 7:00 to 13:00, level 6 pour postponed, crane stood down" is strong.

Say that out loud now.

A daily report must say what stopped, for how long, and whether it was critical, or it proves nothing.

Step 4: the owner change and the time impact analysis

The 15 compensable days came from one owner change: a redesign of the mechanical risers in month 9. The time impact analysis used the schedule update with a data date of day 270, the date to which progress had been recorded. A fragnet was inserted: owner's revised design 8 days, contractor's shop drawings 6 days, review 4 days and extra installation 2 days, a chain of 20 days. That chain sat on a path with 5 days of total float, spare time before it would delay completion. The impact on completion: 20 minus 5 equals 15 days.

Two decisions hide in that subtraction. The first is who owned the 5 days of float. Week 50 taught that if the contract says float belongs to the project, the owner can use it first; if it belongs to the contractor, the owner's change would have been charged the full 20 days. Here the contract said float is shared and available to whichever party needs it first, so the 5 days were consumed by the change. The second is the data date: run the same fragnet on an older update and the float might have been different.

Records needed: the monthly update at the data date, the fragnet with its durations and logic, the float ownership clause, and the dates the owner issued the redesign.

Step 5: the window analysis and concurrency

The contractor's own 10 days of delay came from late window deliveries in months 14 and 15. Was any of it concurrent with the owner change or the weather? A window analysis divided the job into monthly windows. The owner change affected windows 9 to 11, the weather windows 6, 7 and 12, and the windows were late in 14 and 15. They did not overlap, so no concurrency applied, and each delay was assigned to its cause. Had the late windows fallen in months 9 to 11, the contract's concurrency clause would have decided whether those days were compensable at all.

Records needed: a schedule update every month, kept unaltered, and a procurement log showing promised and actual delivery dates.

Step 6: the money

Compensable days: 15 times the contract rate for extended general conditions of 6,000 dollars a day equals 90,000 dollars. That rate was agreed in the contract as a daily figure for owner-caused delay, which saved a fight over the contractor's actual site costs. The direct cost of the riser change was agreed separately by change order. The net settlement: the owner pays 90,000 dollars for time plus the change's direct cost, and deducts 50,000 dollars of liquidated damages, for a net of 40,000 dollars on time.

A forward check. The owner's own daily delay cost was 9,000 dollars a day. Its 15 days of compensable delay cost it about 135,000 dollars of its own money on top of the 90,000 paid to the contractor. The riser redesign, priced as a change at the time with its time effect, would have shown a true cost of the direct work plus about 225,000 dollars. Seen early, the owner might have chosen a different design.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a schedule that is not updated monthly or is altered after the fact, which leaves no contemporaneous basis for any of these steps. The control is a contract requirement for monthly updates, submitted in native format, with each version archived unchanged.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner counts delay in days on site rather than days on the critical path, and pays for time that never moved completion.

Professional sign-off required: scheduling consultant, on the analysis; construction lawyer, on float ownership, concurrency and the settlement terms.

Callback

In Week 82, Vera taught document control: every version kept, nothing overwritten. Every step here depended on one archived schedule update, one daily report or one contract clause. The settlement was only as good as the archive.

Recap

Working backward: total delay from baseline to substantial completion, split into excusable and non-excusable; weather measured against the contract allowance; owner change measured by a fragnet less float; concurrency tested window by window; money from contract rates. Each figure depended on a record created during the job.

Next: Marco on The Room: the claim meeting, when the contractor puts a delay claim on the table.
checklist: I accept a reviewed baseline schedule before work begins.
The contract states a weather allowance by month from historical data.
Daily reports record what stopped, for how long and whether it was critical.
The contractor submits monthly updates in native format, archived unchanged.
Float ownership is written into the contract.
Every owner change is analysed with a fragnet on the current update.
The contract sets a daily rate for extended general conditions on owner-caused delay.
I keep a procurement log of promised and actual delivery dates.
head: Field checklist
speak: We start from the award and work back. The contractor got 25 days of extension, 15 compensable, and paid 10 days of liquidated damages. Total delay was 535 minus 500, 35 days, from an accepted baseline to a certified substantial completion. Ten of the excused days were weather: 22 recorded rain days on critical work against a contract allowance of 12. Fifteen were an owner riser redesign: a fragnet of 20 days inserted into the month 9 update, less 5 days of shared float, gives 15. A monthly window analysis showed the contractor's own late windows did not overlap, so there was no concurrency, and its 10 days carried liquidated damages of 5,000 a day. The money came from a contract daily rate of 6,000 for extended general conditions. Every one of those numbers depended on a record made during the job: the baseline, daily reports, monthly updates kept unchanged, the float clause and a procurement log.
terms: Data date — the date to which progress has been recorded in a schedule update, from which remaining work is calculated.
Total float — the time an activity can slip before it delays project completion.
Extension of time — an agreed or awarded adjustment of the contract completion date for excusable delay.

hostile.q: Your analysis says the owner change cost 15 days. Ours says 20. Why do you get to use the 5 days of float?
hostile.a: Because the contract says float is shared and available to whichever party needs it first, and on the month 9 update, the one in force when the redesign was issued, that path had 5 days of float. I am happy to walk through the fragnet logic line by line. If you think a different update should be used, show me why it better reflects the state of the job at the time.

title: The Claim Meeting: When the Contractor Puts a Delay Claim on the Table
summary: A realistic meeting in which the contractor presents a large delay and disruption claim near completion. The lesson gives the lines to say and never to say, the question behind the question, when to stay silent, and how to move from a demand to an analysis without conceding anything. A monthly thread on decision journals closes it.
body:
The claim meeting is not where you decide the claim; it is where you decide how it will be decided, and the owner who controls the process controls most of the outcome.

Recall

Q. In the reverse-engineered award, why did the owner change cost 15 days rather than 20?

A. Because the fragnet's 20-day chain sat on a path with 5 days of total float, and the contract made float shared and available to the first party who needed it.

Q. What should you do in a pay application meeting if it stops being about facts?

A. End it calmly, arrange a joint site walk, and reconvene at a set time. Ending a meeting is not losing it.

Q. What is a stored materials condition you should never waive?

A. Transfer of title, usually by a bill of sale, together with insurance naming the owner, identification and inspection, before paying for materials not yet built in.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a large claim usually arrives late, often as the contractor sees its own costs. The first meeting sets the tone for everything after. Owners who react, either by arguing or by promising, lose ground they rarely recover. This is a scene with hypothetical people and numbers.

The setting

Month 17 of an 18-month contract. The contractor's commercial director, its project manager and a claims consultant arrive with a bound document: a request for 70 days of extension and 2,400,000 dollars for extended general conditions, acceleration and disruption. Your side: you, Petra as scheduling consultant, and your quantity surveyor. Your lawyer has reviewed the claim overnight and is available by phone, not in the room, which keeps the meeting commercial.

The opening

Begin by framing the meeting, not the claim. "Thank you for the document. Today I want to understand it, not respond to it. We will give you a written response within the period the contract allows, after Petra has reviewed the schedule analysis and our quantity surveyor the costs. What I'd like from today is the basis for each part."

That line does three things: it acknowledges, it gives a date, and it removes the pressure to answer on the spot.

The lines to say

Ask for structure, not argument. "Which schedule update is your analysis based on? Which events do you say were owner-caused, and in which windows? How have you treated your own delays? How are the costs calculated: actual records, or a formula?" Each question is neutral. Each tells you whether the claim is built on contemporaneous records or on reconstruction.

Acknowledge what is true. If your late riser redesign caused delay, say so: "We accept the riser redesign affected the schedule. The question is by how much, and what else was happening in the same windows." Acknowledging the true part gives your challenge to the rest credibility.

Say that out loud now.

Today I want to understand the claim, not answer it. You will have our written response within the contract period.

The lines never to say

Never say "We'll look after you at the end." That is a promise to pay, made without analysis, and it will be quoted back to you. Never say "This is ridiculous." Even if parts are, it ends the conversation and suggests you have not read it. Never say "We'll never pay for disruption." You may have to, and an absolute position invites escalation. And never agree a number in the room.

The question behind the question

A claim this size near completion often carries one of three hidden questions. Is the contractor losing money on the job and trying to recover it? Does it want liquidated damages waived as the real prize? Or does it need cash now to finish? Each needs a different response. You can ask directly: "Is the liquidated damages position the priority for you, or the cost recovery?" Then stay silent. The answer usually tells you where a settlement lies.

A worked example of using that answer. Suppose the commercial director says the liquidated damages matter most. You know your liquidated damages exposure is 40 days at 5,000 dollars a day, 200,000 dollars, and Petra's early view is that 20 to 30 of the 70 days are genuinely owner-caused. A settlement that grants a reasoned extension, removing most liquidated damages, and pays only proven direct costs, may resolve a 2,400,000 dollar demand for a fraction of it. You do not offer it in the room. You note it.

When to stay silent

Stay silent after each question, after they name a number, and after any statement that sounds like a threat, such as "We'll take this to arbitration." The calm reply, after a pause, is: "That is your right under the contract. I'd rather we understand it properly first."

Holding your state

A bound claim is designed to impress. Do not leaf through it in the meeting looking for a weakness. Keep your notes to the questions above. Breathe slowly between answers, sit back, and let Petra and the quantity surveyor do the technical questioning. Your job is the frame.

Afterwards

The same day, send a short note: claim received on this date, the response date under the contract, the information requested, and a reservation of the owner's rights. Then commission Petra's independent window analysis and the quantity surveyor's cost review. A second worked example of priority: if the analysis supports 25 owner-caused days at the contract daily rate of 6,000 dollars, that is 150,000 dollars plus proven disruption, which becomes your evidence-based position.

Keeping talks and evidence apart

Settlement talks and the formal claim run in parallel, and they need different handling. In many legal systems, communications made in a genuine attempt to settle a dispute can be protected from being used as evidence later, often by marking them as without prejudice or under a settlement privilege, but the rules and their limits vary by jurisdiction and are easy to lose by careless wording [unverified — confirm independently]. The practical rule is that your formal response to the claim states your position on the evidence, while any offer is made separately, in the form your lawyer advises. Never put a concession in a routine site email. Ask counsel before the first settlement conversation how to keep the two channels apart.

Monthly thread: decision journals

A claim is a decision under uncertainty, and it will be reviewed later by people who know the outcome. Before you choose a settlement range, write a short decision journal entry: what you know, what you do not, the options, the range you would accept and why, your confidence, and what would change your mind. Week 2 introduced the decision journal as a habit for judgment.

The value is honesty with yourself. When the arbitration or settlement ends, compare the entry with the result. You will learn whether your instinct on claims runs optimistic or pessimistic, and you will have a record that shows the decision was reasoned at the time, which lenders, partners and auditors respect.

Professional sign-off required: construction lawyer, on the response and any reservation of rights; scheduling consultant and quantity surveyor, on the analysis.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is answering the claim in the room. The control is a written process: receipt, information request, independent analysis, written response inside the contract period.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner dismisses the whole claim because part of it is inflated, and then has to concede the true part later from a weaker position.

Callback

In Week 66, Kema and JAX taught interests versus positions. The claim's 2,400,000 dollars is a position. The contractor's interest may be liquidated damages relief or cash flow. Finding the interest is the question behind the question.

Recap

Frame the meeting as understanding, not answering. Ask for the basis of each part, acknowledge what is true, never promise or agree a number in the room, find the interest behind the position, and follow up in writing with an independent analysis.

Next: Kema on the Week 118 review: six questions, a Red Pen drill on a change order, and a two-minute boardroom drill.
checklist: I frame the claim meeting as understanding, with a written response date.
I ask which schedule update and windows the analysis uses.
I ask how the contractor treated its own delays.
I acknowledge any owner-caused delay that is true.
I never promise to pay or agree a number in the room.
I ask what matters most: liquidated damages relief or cost recovery.
I send a written note the same day with a reservation of rights.
I write a decision journal entry before choosing a settlement range.
head: Field checklist
speak: The claim meeting is where I decide how the claim will be decided, not the claim itself. I open by saying I want to understand it today and will respond in writing within the contract period. Then I ask for structure: which schedule update, which windows, how the contractor treated its own delays, and whether the costs come from records or a formula. I acknowledge what is true, such as our own late redesign, because that makes my challenge to the rest credible. I never promise to look after them, never call it ridiculous, never take an absolute position and never agree a number in the room. I ask the question behind the question: is liquidated damages relief the priority, or cost recovery? Then I stay silent. The same day I send a note with the response date and a reservation of rights, commission an independent analysis, and write a decision journal entry before choosing my settlement range.
terms: Disruption — loss of productivity caused by an event, distinct from delay to completion, which must be proved separately.
Global claim — a claim that totals costs without linking each to a specific cause, generally harder to prove.
Decision journal — a written record, made before a decision, of what you know, the options, your choice, your confidence and what would change your mind.

hostile.q: We've given you a fully documented claim for 2,400,000 dollars. If you won't commit today, we'll start arbitration. What's your answer?
hostile.a: My answer is that you will have a written response inside the contract period, based on an independent window analysis and a cost review, and that we already accept the riser redesign affected the schedule. Starting arbitration is your right. I think we will both do better understanding the analysis first, and I'd rather spend the next three weeks on that than on lawyers.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 118 Review: Changes, Notices, Delay and Claims
summary: Six questions test the week's core ideas on changes and claims. A Red Pen drill marks up a hypothetical change order with planted defects. A two-minute boardroom drill closes the week.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: price every change in money and days before the work, answer every notice in writing on time, and measure delay on a live schedule while it happens.

Recall

Q. In the claim meeting, what is the question behind the question when a contractor brings a large claim near completion?

A. Usually whether its priority is relief from liquidated damages, recovery of costs on a losing job, or cash to finish. Each points to a different settlement.

Q. What does a step-down do to retainage?

A. Stops further retainage once measured work passes a set percentage, usually the halfway point, while keeping what was already held.

Q. What does a pile load test prove?

A. That a pile carries its design load with acceptable movement, confirming or adjusting the design assumptions from the geotechnical report before production piling relies on them.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, changes and claims are where projects quietly lose their margin. If you can answer these six questions without notes, you can control a change log and hold your ground in a claim meeting. Answer each aloud before reading the answer, then work the Red Pen drill on paper and time the boardroom drill.

The six questions

Question 1. What is the difference between a change order, a change directive and a claim?

Answer: A change order is signed agreement on scope, price and time. A change directive is the owner's instruction to proceed before price or time is agreed. A claim is a demand for time or money the other side has not accepted.

Question 2. Name the four kinds of delay and what each gives the contractor.

Answer: Excusable non-compensable, time only. Excusable compensable, time and money. Non-excusable, neither, with liquidated damages for late completion. Concurrent, treated according to the contract and governing law, often time without money.

Question 3. Why does only critical path delay move the completion date?

Answer: Because the critical path is the longest chain of linked activities that sets completion. Delay to an activity with float uses the float first and only moves completion if it exceeds it.

Question 4. How can an owner lose the benefit of a time bar?

Answer: By conduct that waives strict compliance, such as negotiating or paying late claims on their merits without reserving rights. Invoke the bar promptly in writing if you mean to rely on it.

Question 5. Why does owner-caused delay cost the owner roughly twice as much as contractor-caused delay?

Answer: Because the owner bears its own daily cost and also pays the contractor's extended general conditions, instead of recovering liquidated damages.

Question 6. State Rule 118.

Answer: Answer every notice in writing inside the contract period, keep an updated schedule that can measure delay as it happens, and price time with every change before the work proceeds.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Marco framed every change as a price and a date and introduced the time impact analysis. Ford and Cole took a composite case of an owner who left delay notices unanswered and lost its concurrency defence. Roman built a daily delay cost and compared it with liquidated damages and acceleration. LEX explained notice, time bars, the prevention principle and concurrent delay. Petra reverse engineered an extension of time from the award back to the records. Marco ran the claim meeting and added the decision journal.

Red Pen drill

Here is a hypothetical change order summary. Find the defects before reading on.

Change Order 14: Upgrade lobby finishes. Price: 180,000 dollars, as quoted by the contractor. Time: to be discussed at the end of the job. Signed for the owner by the site superintendent of the contractor, as the owner's representative was away. This change order is full and final settlement of all matters relating to the lobby. The contractor reserves its rights in respect of delay.

The defects. First, the price is the contractor's quote, with no evidence it was reviewed by the quantity surveyor. Second, time is deferred, which is the single most expensive omission in change control; a time impact analysis should accompany it. Third, it is signed for the owner by the contractor's own superintendent, who has no authority to bind the owner; only a person named in the owner's written authority limits should sign. Fourth, it claims to be full and final settlement while the contractor reserves its rights on delay, so the two sentences contradict each other and the delay remains open. Fifth, there is no description of scope precise enough to measure: upgrade lobby finishes could mean anything. Five defects, each from this week.

Now rewrite it correctly. A model: "Change Order 14: lobby finishes changed from specification A to specification B per drawing revision 3. Price 165,000 dollars as reviewed by our quantity surveyor. Time: 0 days, supported by the attached time impact analysis on the month 11 update, the work being off the critical path. Signed by the owner's authorised representative under the authority schedule. This change order settles all cost and time for the described scope."

Boardroom drill

Set a timer for two minutes. A lender asks: "How do you stop changes and delay claims from eating the contingency?" Answer aloud, then compare with the model.

The model answer: "We treat every change as a price and a date. No change order is signed without our quantity surveyor's price review and a time impact analysis on the current monthly update, and only people named in our authority schedule can sign. Every notice from the contractor is logged the day it arrives and answered in writing inside the contract period, and we give our own notices on time. The contract states float ownership, concurrency treatment and a daily rate for extended costs, so the arguments are settled before they start. We know our own daily delay cost, which today is about 9,000 dollars, so we can decide quickly whether to accelerate or absorb. And our scheduling consultant reviews each monthly update, so if a claim comes, we answer it with contemporaneous analysis rather than reconstruction."

Score yourself: bottom line first, change control, notices, the contract terms, the daily cost, finished in two minutes.

Kema's coaching note

The question that catches most people is the time bar one, because it feels like a technicality. It is not. Practise saying the sentence you would write: we note your notice was received outside the contract period and we reserve our rights, including under the time bar, while we review the matter. Say it until it sounds normal, not hostile. If the delay classification question felt loose, draw four boxes on a page tonight, write one real-world example in each from your own experience on site or on the grid, and say aloud what each box gives the contractor. Concrete examples you chose yourself stick far better than definitions you read. Then record the boardroom drill twice, a day apart, and listen for whether you said a price and a date in the first twenty seconds.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is signing changes for money only. The control is no change order without a time line and a time impact analysis.

The beginner's mistake

Thinking a claim is about who worked slower. It is about the contract, the schedule and the records.

Callback

In Week 48, Marco taught the owner's decision log and approval authorities. The Red Pen change order was signed by someone with no authority, which the Week 48 authority schedule exists to prevent.

Recap

Price changes in money and days, answer every notice on time, classify delay as it happens, measure it on a live schedule, know your daily delay cost, and control the claim process rather than reacting to the claim.

Name the four kinds of delay and what each gives the contractor.
Why does only critical path delay move the completion date?
How can an owner lose the benefit of a time bar?

head: The six questions
speak: This week came down to one sentence: price every change in money and days before the work, answer every notice in writing on time, and measure delay on a live schedule while it happens. A change order agrees scope, price and time; a directive orders work first; a claim is a dispute. Delay is excusable without money, excusable with money, non-excusable, or concurrent, and only critical path delay moves completion. Notice provisions can bar late claims, but conduct can waive a bar, so I invoke it promptly and reserve my rights. Owner-caused delay costs me about twice what contractor delay does, so preventing it is worth more than pursuing the other. In a claim meeting I seek to understand, not answer, and I find the interest behind the number. Rule 118: answer every notice in writing inside the contract period, keep an updated schedule that can measure delay as it happens, and price time with every change.
terms: Construction change directive — the owner's written instruction to proceed with changed work before price or time is agreed.
Critical path — the longest chain of linked activities, which sets the project completion date.
Authority schedule — a written list of who may approve or sign which documents and up to what value.

hostile.q: Your change log shows 14 change orders and a contingency that is 60 percent spent at 50 percent complete. How much of the rest is coming as claims?
hostile.a: I can give you a number with a range, not a guess. Each change order carries a time impact analysis, and the open notices total 22 days, of which our scheduling consultant assesses about half as likely owner-caused. At our contract daily rate that is about 66,000 dollars plus direct costs. I will send you the change log, the notice log and the forecast cost to complete this week.
